utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Morning. Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness will be Mr. Rexhep Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. I think Ms. Nilsen has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Good morning witness.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name and birthday for the record.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: My name is Rexhep Krasniqi. I was born on the 5th of May, 1945 in Pagarush village.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Where are you from?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I am from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And could you be more precise, where in Prizren are you from?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From Dushanove.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Do you still live in this village, Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, did you provide a statement to the Office of Prosecution in 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: On the front page of that statement it says 12th of March, 1999. As far as I know, that date is not correct. Do you know when this statement was made?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it should be the 12th of April, not March.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If we could please put on the screen 65 ter number 02378. That's the April -- 12th of March statement, both the Albanian and the English version of the 1999 statement. And zoom in on the first paragraph there, the first page, or the second page, sorry. This is the 2004 statement. You still have the 2004 statement, the Albanian version, which is not the correct statement, usher, it's 1999 statement, Albanian version on the left side. Yes. This is the correct version. Could you get page 2 and the first paragraph there. So the witness is able to read the first paragraph. And also the same on the English version. Thank you. It was the correct page it was just in this version I would also like to have on the second page first paragraph. So the English page is page 30, I'm told, sorry. In e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I wonder if you are able to read the sentence there, the first paragraph starting with: "Then there our Serbian colleagues told us ..." It's in the middle there.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no, I cannot read it. Can you speak in a louder voice, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: It's still not the correct page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem is one that is occurring from time to time, there seems to be a habit of putting the different translations of the one document in one package as one exhibit, and therefore it becomes impossible to bring up more than one until they are separated, which is what is having to happen at the moment. It would be better, of course, for your next trial, Ms. Nilsen, if they were put separately into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I will keep that in mind, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's all part of life's rich experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. If we still are able to turn on page 2 on the English version there on the right side, then I think we are there. Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Are you still not able to read, Mr. Krasniqi, the sentence saying "then our Serbian" -- or saying something about your Serbian colleagues? It is supposed to be on that page.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't say -- it was not our friends that said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: No, I'm asking if you are able to see it to read a sentence. And if you --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no, no. I can hardly read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Okay. But is it correct that you said back in 1999 -- or I can read the English version here: "Then our Serbian colleagues told us that they would kill us if NATO started bombing them." As I understand you have some corrections to this sentence, Mr. Krasniqi, that it was not your Serbian colleagues who told you this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was the army. Not our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Except from the error in this sentence and also the error regarding the date of this 1999 statement, are you satisfied that this information in the statement is a correct reflection of what you remember?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did you also in September 2004 give a statement where you made some additional information?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Have you read through both of these statements so that you are satisfied of -- that they are to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I have read through them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would seek to tender those two statements, Your Honour, they are already in the same 92 bis package of 65 ter 02378.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received as separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 1999 statement, Your Honours, will be assigned P00848, and the 2004 statement will be assigned P00849.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, did you also testify on the 16th of October, 2006 in the Milutinovic et al. case?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, three years ago when I was here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Exactly. Have you been given a chance to review this transcript before you came to court today?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: But, did you speak to the language assistant before you came to court today, I mean, last week, and got the opportunity to read through this?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, the statement I gave, yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm glad to hear that. If I asked you the same questions today that you were asked back in 2006, would you provide me with the same answer then, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, to my recollection and ability, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And I seek to tender also this transcript into evidence, Your Honours. It's 65 ter number 05032.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00850, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I would now read the court summary for the witness, and after that I have just a couple of questions for the witness. The witness lives in Dushanove village, north-west of Prizren town with his wife and four children. The witness has described that on 28th of March, 1999, there was a buildup of Serbian military in his neighbourhood. The witness has described uniforms worn by the Serb forces and the vehicles used by them. The witness and his brother had 60 displaced people from the neighbour villages staying in their houses. When the police came to the witness house and smashed the front door on the 28th of March, 1999. After being assaulted and threatened, all of the people that lived in the house were told to go to Albania. Everyone left the house and went into the yard where the witness and other family members were beaten and robbed. The witness has testified that he saw houses being burned by the Serb forces. They all eventually set off on foot for the Albanian border. The streets were sealed off, causing everybody to go in the same direction in a long convoy. The witness has described seeing a few young men on a tractor on their way to Albania. When these young men saw the Serbian police they jumped off the tractor and ran away, but the police fired automatic weapons at them, and these young men were immediately killed. At the border, Serbian police confiscated all the identity documents of the civilians. And this is the end of the court summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you have explained in your statement from 1999 that during your six-hour walk towards the Albanian border there were many check-points along the way. I would like to ask you, who were in charge of these check-points? Who were manning them?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And then you mean the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course, the Serb police. There was no one else there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And what did you have to do at these check-points? What did they require from you?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We didn't dare turn our heads right around or left because they would have killed us if we dared do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did they ask you for anything at these check-points?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Whatever we had on us, they took away from us. First they took away whatever we had in our yards and we were left with nothing. We simply were in a convoy of people and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did you have to stop at each and every of these check-points?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, they stopped us at every one of these check-points.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: You also have in your statement explained what happened in the last check-point, before you reached Albanian border. Did you have any documents confiscated before you passed this last check-point?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, but not ours because there was not time for us. They drove us away from work by force, but they took away the others' documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did you personally -- were you personally confiscated any documents? Did you personally have to give away any documents at this check-point?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness answered this for the second time, therefore I have no reason to object any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did you see what kind of document were confiscated from the others?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The ID cards, the licence plates, everything. They confiscated them from these people. They also confiscated their cars when they had cars with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: You said in your statement back in 1999, the last paragraph, that you would go home right now if you thought it was safe. When did you finally return back to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I returned to Kosovo on the 20th of June, 1999. After NATO troops entered Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Nilsen. Mr. Djurdjic, do you cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krasniqi. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, I'm a member of the Defence team of the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic. With me is Ms. Marie O'Leary, a member of the team. Mr. Krasniqi, you said you were born in Pagarusa, can you tell us what municipality that is?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Pagarusha is part of Malishev municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many brothers and sisters did you have?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We are three bother brothers and two sisters. One is dead so now there are only two brothers and two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your parents live in Pagarusa back in 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have some property or land in Pagarusa?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, we do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does your father hail from Pagarusa?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, from Pagarushe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He was a farmer. He worked in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened with his land?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We sold our father's land, and we went to Dushanove, to Prizren. We bought a new place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was that that you went to Dusanovo and bought land there?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was on the 11th of March, 1968 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said 1969, I believe, whereas we have 1968 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, who did you buy the land from in Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We bought the land from Nesahit Recani, from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: One of your brothers died, but was he still alive in 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did one of your brothers work at Prizren Trans?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned one brother in your statement as having been with you. Did you live together?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, we were -- we lived separately. Of course, we were in the same compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was your brother's name, the one who lived with you?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The one who is dead, Mehmed Krasniqi; the other is Shefqet Krasniqi; and you know my name, Rexhep Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was Mehmed's occupation?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Odd jobs, whatever he could find. He was a bricklayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It says here that your other brother was Rexhep Krasniqi. Let's correct that. One of your brother's name is Mehmed Krasniqi, and what was the other brother's name?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Shefqet Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was Shefqet's occupation?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He worked in the construction business. Now, he is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did all of you live in the same compound but in different houses?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krasniqi, what schooling do you have?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Eight years of schooling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can see that you worked in Printex for a number of years. What jobs did you work at?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, in the textile industry where they produce threads, the weaving sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What were your jobs there?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We called the place "batere" where the cotton was processed. The first process.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was general manager of Printex in 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Mile. In our workshop, it was Mile who was the manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But what about the entire company, the entire factory of Printex?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Faruk Mermeri.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He was a general director. Mile was the manager of our workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the general manager before Faruk Mermeri?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were rotated; Sadedin was one. There were many there, because I worked there for 34 years so we had several general managers. Luftim Demiri was another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm surprised to hear that you don't know that back in 1999 it was Vojkan Zecovic who was the general manager.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is possible. We didn't have contact with him. If he is a person who moved there from another factory, then it can be him as well. But I cannot tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, he was at the factory from the establishment of Printex, and he was there even when Demiri, the legendary director, was at the head of the enterprise.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, he was. Faruk Mermeri as well, many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me about that estate where you lived. Did the yard have a wall around it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me what was it made of, this fence? How tall was it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was built of concrete blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How high was it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: 1.80 metres high.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me, when did you do your military service and where?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I completed my military service in Niksiq. From there we were transferred to Bosnia to watch The Battle at Neretva movie, and then I returned again. I completed it in 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the name of your street in Dusanovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Boulevard i Rinise, 154. The names are now being changed, but it is in my statement, the name of the street I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is your street from the main road to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not more than 200 metres. That should be the distance. I didn't measure it, but it should be about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it runs parallel to the road, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We call it the Transit Road now that links up with the main road going to Jakova and to the town. That's the part I was referring to when I said 200 metres far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just saying your street runs parallel to the road.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: To get on to the main road you have to turn left into a side-street and then --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You have to take a turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see the road from your house, the Djakovica-Prizren road?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it, but there is a house right in front of our house that impedes the view, blocks the view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But within those 200 metres, are there any more houses?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, there are. From the main road to the road where my house is, there is a row of houses; and then where my house is, there are other houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know Uni Hakic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, not in my neighbourhood. Perhaps there is someone by that name, but there are many people residing there, so I don't know all of them by names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dusanovo is part of Prizren, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it's part of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it is on a plain?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is adjacent to Prizren. It's a neighbourhood of Prizren. It's not separate from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. I'm just saying that this part of Prizren is on level ground. Your neighbourhood Dusanovo is in the field of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is a plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From Dusanovo, can you see Bazdarana?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, but now you can't see it because there are higher blocks of flats that block the view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You mean Ortokol. And when were you able to see Bazdarana from Dusanovo? In which year?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Now, you could not see it. You could see it then. Now there are many more houses built there, so you cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you when were you able to see it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You could see it about 30 years ago when these apartment blocks were not built there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's what I was asking. Is it right that from Dusanovo you cannot see the barracks that are situated by the road from Suva Reka to Prizren?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Now you cannot see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You could see it 30 years ago?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, you could see them very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you stop working at Printex?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I stopped working in 2004 because the factory was closed down and we remained jobless.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I mean in March 1999, did you continue working there up to the moment when you left Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I worked there until the bombing started. And when I returned from Albania to Kosova in June, I continued working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did you notice before the 24th of March that people were leaving Prizren, going away?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Before the 24th? Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that people were leaving Prizren before the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that anyone left Dusanovo before the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in terms of ethnic structure, what kind of people live in Prizren, and what languages do they speak?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about Turks?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, there weren't any Turks. There were Gorans, Albanians, and Serbs living together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go into the building of the municipal assembly of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Are you referring to the old one or to the newly built one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, when I talk, I talk always about 1998 and 1999, because that's the relevant period for us. I'm asking you questions up to 1999. Did you ever go into the town hall, or to the SUP building, or the survey department building, any building of the local administration?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the municipal office because whenever we needed a document to be issued to us, we had to refer to that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you never saw a notice, a board on the municipal building written in the Turkish language?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, when we would go to the municipal building, we could use the three languages, the Serb language, Albanian language, and Turkish. We could use the three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that is why I'm asking, because the Turkish language could be used as well. And you said a moment ago the Turks lived in Prizren in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, there are still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And one of the towns' languages is Turkish. But tell me about the village of Mamusa, which you mentioned in your statement. What is the majority population of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Turkish is also spoken in Mamusha village. I mentioned Mamusha in terms of the people who were droven [as interpreted] away from there and who had to come towards our neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The majority population of Mamusa are the Turks; am I right?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The population is mixed, Albanians living there, Turks too. A new municipality has been formed there, but they still live there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt, I would just like the witness to clarify a bit regarding the Turks he is mentioning in Prizren. On the question from my learned colleague he said that there were no Turks living in Prizren, and then he was confronted that he said that there was living a large number of them. I'm not sure whether he is talking about Mamusa or Prizren. If the witness could clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, the witness did give two quite contradictory answers about Turks living in Prizren. Perhaps you might determine which is correct. Were there Turks living in Prizren or were there not, and were they living in large numbers, if there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that everything entered on to the record is the result of the cross-examination. From the answer that there were no Turks to the other answer that there were Turks in large numbers. I think Ms. Nilsen should deal with it in redirect if she wishes. In my view, everything is clear. When I asked him the question about boards, he answered clearly what the situation was in Mamusa, and now I moved on to another place. If you think this requires clarification, I will seek it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You carry on then, Mr. Djurdjic. We put the problem to you. If you think it's best left as it is, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Witness, that a considerable number of people of Turkish ethnicity lived in Prizren in 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I cannot hear very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, am I right that there was a considerable number of Turks living in Prizren? I mean Turks by ethnicity, by origin.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This would be my answer, those who speak Turkish I consider them Turks. I don't know their exact number, the exact figure of Turks living there. I only know that those who speak Turkish are Turks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And am I right that in all public buildings in Prizren there were signs in three languages; in Albanian, in Serbian, and in Turkish?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And concerning Mamusa, I told you that the Turks were the majority population there in 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There are more Turks living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From those people who arrived on the 26th or 27th March to Prizren, did you hear that there had been fighting in that area?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When they came from Mamusha on the 27th in the evening, I didn't hear anything about that. And you probably know, sir, that Mamusha is not very far from Dushanove; it's about 17 kilometres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And how far is Pirane from Prizren, or from Dusanovo, whatever?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: About 10 kilometres far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about Mali Krushe?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Krusa e Madhe, it's about 15 kilometres away. It's a little bit further on the road to Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about Landovica?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: 3 kilometres from our village Xerxe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How far is Celine?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Celina is closer than Xerxe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And until the 28th of March, you did not hear that in all these villages or in areas overlooking these villages, fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There weren't any fighting in our neighbourhood. On the other parts, you can hear the noise of the military vehicles. You could hear the firing on a daily basis. Shelling, tanks, all sorts of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how do you know whose weapons those were?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We knew that because when the forces would target the villages that were further away, they would use the 105 millimetre weapons, whereas they would use smaller calibre weapons for the villages that were closer to our neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I know because the 105 millimetre cannons are used for distant targets. I know this from the time I served my military service. And you can tell the difference from the sound as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was your specialty in the army?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And where did you see a cannon?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly when I saw a cannon for a first time. I've been going to Belgrade from 1963. I've seen all different types of weapons and weaponry, so I can tell the difference. That I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how do you distinguish -- even if I accept that you distinguish between weapons by sound, but how can you distinguish who is firing those guns?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I know that the military forces always attacked the people, and that's why I knew where they were firing, where they were positioned. It was only the army and the police that had those types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you wanted to fight, could you do it on your own, against yourself?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You cannot fight against yourself. I served in the army, but I never pointed my weapon at a civilian. Only those who used their weapons against the civilians know the reasons why they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know what the KLA is?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw KLA members after I arrived in Albania on television. Otherwise, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you saw them, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw them on television defending their people, defending their own houses, defending their homeland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you like a break at the present time, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I'm willing to continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, do let us know if you are feeling unwell, won't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me how was it that they were defending their own houses and defending their homeland?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Please, I'm here to discuss my statement, and I can tell you everything related to my statement. I can give you an answer, but I don't think the questions you are making now are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'd be grateful if you would help us by answering these questions, Mr. Krasniqi. We have to decide in the light of many things that are being considered in this trial what is relevant, and what is relevant goes beyond your own particular experience. So we'd be grateful to hear your answers. They will help us. Mr. Djurdjic is trying to explore a number of issues wider than the content of your statement perhaps. So it would be appreciated if you could help him by giving some answers, and that in turn will help us. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I was asking you about something from your statement since you provided an answer or two in that regard. Therefore, I would kindly ask you to answer my previous question. How were they defending their homeland and houses? In which way?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I will try to answer your question. If, for example, you are attacked in your own house, you have to defend yourself. So our houses, wherever they stood in fields, on hills, they were attacked; and the KLA was there to protect these houses, to protect that land. I don't know what other answer I can give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you present during --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where did you get that information from then?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: But it is -- everything is clear to everyone. Everything was done in the light of day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me who was a member of the KLA in Dusanovo, or who were members?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I cannot tell you this because simply I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How come then you don't know that they were not active?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I'm telling you, sir, that if what happened to others happened to me, I would have also taken up arms and protected my own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you watch television, in Albania?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We had the television set there, we could follow what was happening in our country, in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In which town were you, and when did you watch television?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was in Kruja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where were you accommodated?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were distributed to different private homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive at Kruje?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We arrived in Kruja on the 28th after we left Dushanove at 5.00, and on the 29th we arrived in Kruja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At what time did you leave Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At 5.00. 4.00 or 5.00 we left. We were actually forced to leave and go towards the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At what time did you reach the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... hundred. At 1100.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many kilometres are there between Dusanovo --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They say 18, but I think 16, around about the same figure. I think 18 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Dusanovo, were there any Serb families there?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which families do you know of?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I know their names. There were about 40 households that lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know anyone's last name?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Boge, Nebojsa, Nidjivki [phoen] there were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: There were many Rexheps and Shefqets, but I would like to know their last names.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know their surnames because we didn't use to call them by their last names. We called them by their first names. It's not -- we spent a lot of time with them, in fact, but we called them by their first names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Between the 24th of March of 1999, and up to the time when you departed, was there any bombing in --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was Prizren struck from the air?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it was struck.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the bombs landed?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The bombs landed in Spilje [phoen], in Kasama [phoen], the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did I hear you correctly as having said Svilene?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same. We are talking about the same bombing. Some may call it Spilje, some may spell it differently, but it's the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure. You said that the barracks were bombed. Were the barracks in town?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was in the outskirts of Prizren, on the road to Suhareke. It's on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you understood what I meant. Can you tell me who was the chief of police in Prizren of the police station?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where is the Printex factory?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The Printex factory is below the railway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the industrial part?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did you see tanks on the Printex factory compound?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw them on the 23rd of March when we went to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What did the tanks look like?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The tanks were the tanks of the army of green colour, the army tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How many tanks did you see?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't count them. I couldn't give you an accurate figure, but I would say about 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the war in 1999, what kind of uniforms did police wear in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The police had kind of dark blue uniform. I'm talking about the period before the war. After the war, they had the same but they had also camouflage colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: After what war?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: During the war. I'm saying they had this camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniform for me?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: How can I describe it? How can I describe it here? I don't know how. You show me something, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's try it this way: What does camouflage uniform mean to you?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: By this I mean that it is not a solid colour, but it's a colour with patches. How can I say it to you? It is different from the uniforms of the army. It's not the same. It's a mixture of colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said they had patches, but what were the hues, the colours of the fabric?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: How can I explain it to you now? Some were of lighter colours, some were of darker hues. Patches were of a darker colour compared to those of the army. How can I say? I don't know how.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what was the colour for the army?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was of green, and the patches were bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see any other uniforms apart from the two?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You are asking me to distinguish the colours. When we were forced to leave the houses, I saw dark colours, black colours, masked faces. All sorts of colours. It was only on the day that they attacked us, they forced us to leave the houses. I saw people dressed in black colours and wearing masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you trying to tell us that apart from these two types of uniforms there was a third one you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me, these persons wearing the dark or black uniforms, what kind of insignia did they have?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Didn't have any insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who did the black uniformed troops belong to? Which organisation?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The police, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Based on what are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Even though I could answer the question you are asking of me, I may say that usually they stayed with the police forces, but I think they were even more dangerous because I think they belonged to special intervention units. At least, this is what people said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that? Somebody told you?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Nobody told me this. Nobody told me. But we lived through all these things. It doesn't matter whether it was the police, the army, the Arkan's forces, however, we suffered from them. They beat us up, they forced us it to leave, they killed us, so for us it doesn't matter what unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You just said Arkan's forces. What kind of forces were they, and where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't see these forces, but whenever we saw that force was being used, we thought that these forces belonged to Arkan, to this or to that, so I couldn't say that these forces belonged to me for example, because I didn't have such forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever heard or did you see that the KLA's military police wore black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw the KLA uniforms only on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of March in the morning, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 27th of March, I went out to the main street, and I heard the noises of the shelling and nothing else. Nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When exactly when you got out into the street?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We went out several times. Whenever we heard there was a commotion, a noise, we wanted to see what was happening, where the population was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But tell me, that morning, what were you doing before you went into the street? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I woke up in the morning after sleeping. I went out. I did the same thing that everybody does when you go out, trying to meet someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the time when you got up?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, please, I don't remember when I woke up this morning. How can I remember when I woke up ten years ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who were you supposed to meet?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We didn't have particular meetings, you know. I didn't have anyone to meet. I simply went out to see what was going on outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You answered me "trying to meet someone"?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean, you come across some neighbours, some friends from another neighbourhood, from your neighbourhood, you ask what he is doing, what has he been doing and so on. Things like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it already day?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I'm not clear about your question. Are you asking me about the morning or about the evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that morning and when you got out into the street, had it dawned already?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, it was daylight. We don't wake up in the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far did you go from your house?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From my street to the main street, I already explained earlier on, it is only 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just give me a brief answer. I don't know where you went when you left your house. When you left your house, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When I left my house, as usual, even today, I go out, walk around for 200 metres, go to the main street that links Prizren with Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must have a break now, Mr. Krasniqi, it will give you time to improve your feeling. We will resume in half an hour and the court officer will assist you during the break. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, we reached the moment when you got out of your house and went to the main road. Can you tell me if you ran into anyone? Did you talk to anyone?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke with my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where did you meet up, and where did you talk?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, we exchanged greetings, discussed if they saw anything on TV, what were the news, what was going on. That sort of talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I then went back home. They went back to their own homes, to their own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you then do in your own house?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The usual work I do at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the situation completely normal at the time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, it wasn't completely normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but tell me what was going on.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Of course, the situation was not normal. You could hear noises on all sides, people would say -- would tell us what was going on. There was fighting. It wasn't normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you said you went back home, you talked to people, exchanged whatever you exchanged, and then you went back home?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I did go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I did my usual work around the house, and on the evening of the 27th, we went out to the place where we usually stayed together, on the main road, saw the convoys of people coming towards us, people that had been expelled from Mamusha village. We knew some of the people in that convoy. We invited them to stay in our village because there was nothing going on in our village. They stayed that night, in our village. And on the following day, big forces came, they positioned themselves on the main crossroads. So I think I'm answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are not answering my question. I don't want to hear you telling stories. We came to the point when you came back home from that intersection, and I'm asking you what happened then at your home. What was going on? Let's not waste time, please answer my questions as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I think I answered your question. When I came back home, I did my usual work around the house. There were shelling and gun-fire that was heard. There was no other discussion at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of work did you do, and what was the time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I told you, it was morning when I went out. I returned home, did some work in the garden. I could hear the sound of gun-fire. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We stayed in the house until the evening, then we went out to the same place, to the main road, and we saw the convoy of people coming from the direction of Mamusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not asking you about the evening of the 27th. I'm asking you about the morning of the 28th, and as far as I understand, you are answering now questions about the morning of the 28th. I'm not interested in the evening of the 27th. I'm interested in that morning of the 28th. You went to the centre, you came back home, you did some work in your house. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, I think you are mixing up the questions. I thought you were asking me about the 27th when we invited these people to stay in our village. On the 28th, we were first out together with these refugees that came from Mamusha. So please tell me now, are you interested in the morning of the 27th or the morning of the 28th, because I'm not clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The morning of the 27th was not my question. My question was about the morning of the 28th.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, now I will answer your question about this date. On the 28th we woke up earlier than on other dates because we had refugees. We had to prepare some food for them. So it was normal to wake up earlier than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We talked. We discussed the way they were expelled from their village, what happened there. Because in our village there was no police presence until the 28th, that's why we talked about the situation in that village, what made them flee, what else happened, if anyone was killed there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In the evening -- now, do you want me to tell you word by word everything that we discussed until that evening, or what happened that evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I am being interpreted very well, and you understand perfectly well what I'm saying. We are talking about the morning of the 28th. I'm asking you only about that, nothing else. And please continue to answer my question. What were you doing on the morning of the 28th? You started answering and then I asked you, and then what?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 28th we woke up early in the morning. We talked with the guests staying at our house, discussing the situation in that village. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. You told me that already. And I asked you what happened then, what did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, this was not ten days ago. This was ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you on the basis of your statement what happened later. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I really don't know what answer to give you. You have the right to ask me, and I have the right to answer your question. If you are asking me now what happened on the 28th in the evening, I will answer that. I don't know what else to tell you about the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the evening of the 27th or the 28th. I don't know which dates you are talking about now. I'm asking you about the morning, what happened in the morning, and you are telling me for the third time that you talked to your neighbours, and I'm asking you what happened after that. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness has told you, Mr. Djurdjic, that he remembers nothing specific on the morning of the 28th except at having risen early, helping with the feeding of the people that had stayed overnight. He then talked to them about affairs in their village. Now, that's what the witness remembers about the morning of the 28th. He can remember something about the evening of the 28th, if you want to learn something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I'm asking questions on the basis of the statement that I have in front of me. I'm not interested in just any date. I'm interested in the morning after that evening, and I'm coming back to that morning for the third time because that's when the events began, and the witness keeps coming back to the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There may be some confusion because of your persistence with the particular date, Mr. Djurdjic. Would you like me to try to cut through it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be very happy if you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've told us, Mr. Krasniqi, that police came to your village. Are you able today to remember what date that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The police came on the 28th. On the 27th we offered shelter to the people who came to our village. On the 28th, the police forces entered our village in the afternoon at around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. So I can tell you now about this part of the day because retelling here word by word the discussions I had with the refugees in the morning, and telling the counsel what I ate that morning and all these other small things I did, I wouldn't be able to say everything exactly how it happened, in what consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we all understand that, Mr. Krasniqi. Perhaps you can tell us when you first were aware of police in your village. What did you see or hear that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 28th, since the counsel wants to know what happened, as I said earlier, on the 27th, these refugees came to our village, stayed in our houses. On the 28th we woke up, we discussed the situation in their village, we had something to eat, and we all shared the same concern, what was going to happen, what was going to happen with us, where we would end up. And at around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., there was noise at the gate to the yard. The police entered forcefully into the yard. They didn't ask us anything. They ordered us to raise our hands in the air. They started beating us. They beat my wife, my daughter, my brother, myself. They beat up some refugees. One of them cut a small girl in her throat nearly killing her. So if the counsel is interested in these things, I can tell him everything that happened. I cannot recall everything I ate that day, but these things I recall very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've now moved on, Mr. Krasniqi, to the afternoon at about 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. And you tell us that at that time the -- there was a noise at the gate to your yard, and the police forcefully came into the yard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I understand Mr. Djurdjic would like you to tell us what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the police entered the village, they positioned themselves on the crossroads of the neighbourhood with a tank. They entered my yard forcefully. They didn't ask us anything. They made us raise our hands in the air, pushed us behind the wall, took our money, beat us up, and told us that there was no place for us there in the village, that we had to go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I don't want you to repeat the statement that we already have. I want you to answer my questions. Is it correct that you spent four or five hours at home that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From that time when you went out in the morning and when you talked to the people until 1600 hours, did you spend all that time at home?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I was at home, sir. We had refugees staying with us, as I said, and we stayed there in the house together until the police forces came.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know then what happened with the Serbian families?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know if anything happened to the Serb families. When the NATO bombing started, the following day in the morning we saw that their houses were empty. I don't know where they went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how do you know that the house -- that the village was surrounded because you stayed at home all the time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I knew that because as of the 27th when they had expelled people from Mamusha, there was continuous movement of police and army forces, so we knew that we had them all on our sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me what you personally knew about the movements of the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe this to you, sir. You keep asking me the same questions. I told you several times that I would usually go out to the main street. Not only the time of the war, but on every-day basis almost. So I was able to see this constant movement. And when there was increased movement, we could tell that we were in danger. And now you are asking me why I went out to the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. I just said that you went out in the morning, and this was happening at 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. How did you gain any personal knowledge considering that from the morning until 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., you did not leave your house?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not at 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. what?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't even mention 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning. It was 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. on the 28th when the forces entered the village. I never mentioned the morning of the 4th -- the morning of the 27th or the 28th, 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot explain all of that to you now. It's all in the transcript. But my question was, and please try to focus, you stated that in the morning, you went out onto the main road, then you went back home, and then until 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., you did not leave your home.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct. And I keep saying the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You did not leave your home in that interval?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't leave my house. I would go out to the gate and from there I could see the movement of the police and other forces on the road. And when they entered the village, it was around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From your gate, where did you see the police entering the village?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: As I said, sir, the main road is very close to the gate to my yard, and the crossroads where they positioned themselves is not further than 50 metres from the gate to my yard, and I could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, your street runs parallel to the main road, and you say there are a number of buildings between your house and the main road. Your gate facing the street does not provide a view of the main road?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You cannot see the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how, then, are you able see to that your village is surrounded by the forces?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, as I said earlier, the main road is only 200 metres away from my house. The first road turning to the right is very close to my house. That's a crossroads and that's where they positioned themselves with the tanks, with everything. That crossroads is only 50 metres away from my house. Whereas the main road, the Prizren-Gjakove Road is 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I accept that you saw what you just told me, but how did you see -- how were you able to see that your village was surrounded by any forces, since you have stated that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On both sides of the street there are sidewalks, broad sidewalks, and you can see everything that goes on. You can see even if someone is walking, let alone large number of military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And your street?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In my street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What were you able to see from your gate? Can you describe that for me?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw movements of police forces, and I withdrew, went back to my yard. I entered my yard. I talked with my family, telling them that there is a large police presence and something is going to happen probably. Before I ended my conversation with the family, the police forces entered my yard. They forced the door open and entered my yard. They were about 20 policemen. They didn't ask us anything, only ordered us to raise our hands up, beat up our family members, and drove us out of the family together with those refugees that we sheltered on the 27th that I mentioned earlier. They maltreated us in the yard. So you asked me earlier how do I know. This is how I know. I'm telling you. Since you were not there to experience what I went through, you don't have the right to ask me about the things which I went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you were in the yard when the 20 policemen entered it. Who was in the yard with you?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: My family members and those refugees that I took in the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which of your family members were there?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Myself, my wife, my two daughters, two sons, my daughter-in-law, and their small daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how many people from Mamusha were there that you had taken in?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is answering in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were 28 people there together with my family members, and we were all seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were they in the yard when the police came?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, they were in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the police told you to leave the yard and go out into the street immediately?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, they did many bad things to us, but I'm not in a position to describe to you in detail what we experienced that day. They beat up all of us, but as I said, I am not in a position to tell you everything they did to us that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I don't think anyone beat you up, and that's why you cannot tell us what took place on that day. I put to you that you set out to Kukes because of the fear of being bombed and the fear of war?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, I don't have an answer for your question, which seems to me a very provoking one. I didn't leave because of the NATO air-strikes. I left because of what the Serb forces did to my family and to myself personally. Not because of NATO bombing. Only because of the Serb forces and only because of what they did to us in my yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Then answer my question, please. How long did the 20 policemen stay in your yard before you left?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: If I got you right, when the policemen entered my yard by force, they didn't give us any time to get ready. They forced us to leave in 10 minutes. They entered by force and forced us to leave the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was it daylight when you were forced to leave the yard?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, it was 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. It was still daylight. When they entered the yard, as I told you, I'm repeating it, they didn't ask our opinion. They cut the eight-month baby by the throat and forced us to leave without asking our consents. They simply ordered us to leave and go to Albania. They used violence against us. They said there is no place for you to stay in Kosova, go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you went on foot; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were forced to leave, as I told you. They did not allow us to go back and fetch our identity cards, documents, so we joined the column and went to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which road did you take from your house?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The same road, the main road which was 200 metres away from my house. We joined the column and started to walk in the direction of Albania along the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you turn from the main road?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. We turned left towards Prizren and then straight to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you which road you took through Prizren to Vrmnica. Where did you reach the main road?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From my street to the main road, there are only 200 metres. From -- we met the neighbours and together with went to the main road linking Prizren, that road goes in the direction of Morine, in the direction of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I believe you understand what I'm asking you. You followed the main road, and now I'd like to know which road you took through Prizren to Vrmnica. Which road did you use to go through Prizren?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Why are you not asking me where we went? We went to Prizren, then we took the road that goes towards the industrial plant and that road goes to Dragash-Vermice. You know it better than I. Why are you provoking me, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not trying to provoke you. In order to reach Vrmnica from Dusanovo, one can take two roads through Prizren. I'm asking you which one you took so that I could ask you the next question. I'm not doing this without a reason.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When you enter through the main road, that road which links Prizren-Gjakove, you enter the city. We turn on the right, and we went to -- before entering the city, we entered that street. We couldn't enter the city because the police didn't let us. We went that road that goes to Vermice. I don't know how else can I explain to you other than take you by the hand and take you to the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You needn't do that, Witness. I know the road itself. Did you go through the industrial area next to your factory eventually reaching the hygiene company on the road to Vrmnica?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You could have said so a while ago.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I told you, but you mix it all up with your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We understood the witness to tell us that sometime ago, Mr. Djurdjic. Your questions are not clear either to us or to the witness and they often lead him in a wrong direction in answer. So your last comment was not well justified. If you could carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to be as clear as possible without any hidden intentions. There are only two roads, one through the centre of town and the other one that was confirmed by the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we got through the town, we know the road, could you move on from there, please, whatever your next question may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The tractor you described in your statement, where did you see that along your route?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The tractor I saw when we returned above the school, there is the railway which is parallel to the main asphalt road, we were about 150 metres down before the tractor -- before we went to the tractor. I saw two, three young lads who, upon seeing the police, tried to flee. The police shot them killing two of them, and I am proving it to you, if you believe me, that when we approached that tractor, we saw them falling down in the middle -- in the place between the railway and the road. I hope you understand me, sir. We simply saw them. We didn't dare to do anything because I am afraid they would have done the same to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How far were you from your house when this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: About 1200 metres, I would say, from my house to this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How much time did it take you to cross that distance?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When you walk alone, it might take 15 minutes; but if you are part of a convoy, as I was, it might have taken longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where were the policemen that you say opened fire at those young men?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The policemen were in that place below the school. I'm sure you know the place better than I. I'm telling you, you don't seem to believe what I'm saying, you may verify it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The school is on the left-hand side of the road going the way you were taking?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the left side of the road that goes to Prizren is a school where our kids go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the convoy or the column occupy the whole road along the entire distance you travelled?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it occupied the whole road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The young men you referred to, why did they begin to flee, if you know?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't talk with them. I was far from them. I didn't meet them, but usually the young men fled the police forces because they took them to the barracks, and they never returned them. They used them to do something for them or kill them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: These men were on a tractor that was part of the column; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. They jumped off the tractor when they went to that place I mentioned between the railway and the road; the police killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, the railroad is to the right of road in the direction of where you were going; right?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did they run across the tracks, and did you see them do that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
