utterances.text: No, no, they didn't manage to because there is an empty space of 20, 30 metres between the road and the railway tracks; and it was in that space that they were shot at by the police and killed. So they didn't manage to cross the tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the policemen were next to the school?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, they were next to the school, in the school, in the main road where I turned to Prizren. As I said, the entire neighbourhood was surrounded by police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What time was it when it took place?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I said to you, it was about 4.00, 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You haven't mentioned coming across a check-point. Where was the first check-point you came at?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The first check-point was in our street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What were they doing there, the people manning the check-point?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were police, army forces there, moving about. There were tanks placed at every intersection with cannons 105 millimetres. They were above the tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the next check-point after that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The second was in the school. As I said, at every intersection in our neighbourhood there were forces, even in front of the houses sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the second check-point was in the school itself?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At the school. The third was at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next check-point after that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Every 50 metres, every 20 metres there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what occurred at those check-points?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The worst you can say occurred there. They took people out of the convoy in groups sometimes, and we don't know who the policemen were, and I don't know what happened to them. We know nothing what happened to them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone stop you at the check-points?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were part of the convoy. We didn't leave the column, the convoy, because otherwise we might have been shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Save for the tractor, as you were walking down the main road, did you notice anything else happening?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. We saw people being taken out of the convoy and not returning. We saw villages burned down, houses burned down or houses in flames. All such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the border you saw a policeman you knew from Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, Nebojsa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where was his house in Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether he continually resided in his house in Dusanovo throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Nebojsa, yes, he lived there all his life. I found him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We are talking about Nebojsa Ognjanovic [phoen]; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't remember that, to tell you the truth. I only know that he was working in the customs. He was a policeman there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. His brother was a customs officer at the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no, Nebojsa himself worked at the customs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, where did you give your first statement?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: My first statement was given in Kruje in April. The date of the statement, I don't remember, but when you said that it was the 12th of March, I remembered it was not on that date, but it was on the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I was not the person to say that, but it was rather my learned friend. In any case, who was present on the occasion when you gave that statement? Who did you give the statement to?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When we were there, the place where we were staying, there were two persons, a man and a woman, and the interpreter, a lady, asked me -- I didn't know -- asked me something I didn't know I was supposed to give an interview. I thought she was asking me for someone. And she said to me that this gentleman wants to ask you why you are here and what happened to you and so on. And that was how it came that I gave this statement. She asked me as you are asking me now about these events, and I told them what I'm saying now, these things. Nothing more than what I'm saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I signed it on the 10th or the 13th of December, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who was present?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, it was the first time you saw that statement?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the same person present the second time around as the first time when you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, it was not the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who was there with you the second time when you signed the statement in your house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has already replied to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He has. He has no recollection, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. He does not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But do you remember how many people came to your house on that occasion when they brought your statement with them?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The first time around, there were two of them; and the third time there were three of them in 2004 when some corrections were made on 19th of September, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you born?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was born in Pagarusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No. When were you born?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When I was born?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was born on the 5th of May, 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your personal identification number says that you were born on the 10th of May, 1945.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sir, every document that was issued to me was with a date I gave you, the 5th of May, 1945. All the documents that were issued to me bear this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You never told anyone that there was a mistake in terms of your ID number. You never tried to correct that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, is there any issue about the identity of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, having in mind the statement that was signed and the problems surrounding the year of birth, I'm not convinced that the procedure that was followed was valid. That's why I'm asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not going to assist this Chamber whether the witness was born on the 5th or the 9th of May, 1945, Mr. Djurdjic. There are some issues in the evidence of the witness that are quite material to the question of what occurred in the village and by that means to the question of the guilt or innocence of your client. Could I suggest you concentrate on those instead of an issue such as whether there is a for or five-day error about the date of birth of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm at the very end of my cross-examination, but I'm not certain whether this witness gave this statement in the first place. The only thing I know is that he is sitting here testifying. We've just confirmed that the statement of the 12th of April was not signed as originally stated but that it was signed when they visited him at his house. Concerning the first statement, there is no name of the interpreter, on the second one there is. The signature on the statements from 1999 in April and December seem to me to be different. That's what I wanted the witness to explain. That was the gist of my questions, and I guess he has provided some answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why have you taken the long way around it, Mr. Djurdjic? The witness has looked at the statement has said it is his. Now, if you think it is not his signature and you have some basis for that, ask the witness if it is his signature instead of troubling about an error on the date of birth of the witness. If you want to question the signature, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I don't know how to follow this up. The statement that mistakenly stays the 12th of May [as interpreted] in 1999 was not signed on that day but later as the witness says. And then there's the second statement of December 1999 that he signed. I wanted to ask him about that and he provided some answers. Had I put it another way, he probably would not have provided me with those answers. I apologise for having gone the roundabout way. In any case, I would I like to thank the witness, since this is the end of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Nilsen, do you re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to ask the witness a question regarding the statement he gave in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you have already clarified that that statement you gave in 1999 was given in April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. It was more like an interview. It was not read back to me. However, in December 1999 they showed me the statement, read it out to me, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Exactly. On the very top of the first -- the second page of the statement from April 1999, it says that it is an informal statement of you. Did you have that impression also, as you said, you didn't read through it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's like a conversation they had with me, an interview. I didn't sign anything at that stage. When I returned home after the war, sometime in late 1999, in December, they came, they showed me the statement, read it back to me, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not have any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krasniqi, you'll be pleased to know that that completes the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your assistance here, to the trouble you've taken in coming to The Hague again. And we will give consideration to your evidence in due course. So you may now, of course, return to your ordinary affairs, and the court officer will show you out and you go with our thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is General Maisonneuve. I don't know if Your Honours prefer to start now with the witness. I think we -- yes, we're still 20 minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we should use the 20 minutes that we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read the affirmation on the card shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness, could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Joseph Omar Michel Maisonneuve.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I understand that you are a retired Lieutenant-General from -- with the Canadian forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did you serve with the Canadian forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Exactly 34 years and ten months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while you were in active service, did you spend sometime in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did, probably a total of about 3 months on the ground in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I deployed about the middle of December, 1998, and left in March, middle of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was your function in Kosovo during that period when you were deployed there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I was head of the regional centre that was based in Prizren in the south part of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And to which --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: With the OSCE, pardon me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in relation to your work with the OSCE in Kosovo during this period?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had the chance to review your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having we viewed your statement, are you satisfied that the information contained within this statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly pause between questions and answers for the sake of interpretation and the court reporter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My apologies for that, we'll try to remember to pause. Your Honours, the statement is 65 ter number 02772, and I seek to tender it into evidence. This statement has a series of attachments which we also seek to tender. I do wish to point out that attachment number 1 has already been admitted into evidence. This is Exhibit P836, so we do not seek to tender it again. There are three further attachments which we do not intend to tender. These are attachments 4, 11, and 12 to this witness statement. We have notified Defence of that, and I understand -- I see my learned colleague is on his feet, so I understand he has an observation to make in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no objections. I would like to propose, as in the case of Mr. Ciaglinski, that those exhibits, which were admitted in the Milutinovic case through this witness, and across the bar table, be admitted in this case as well as we did in the case of the previous witness. Hence, I have no objections to what Ms. Kravetz just said. Rather, I propose that we should follow the practice we had with the previous witness as this proved more efficient. If I understood correctly, the Milutinovic case transcript will be admitted into evidence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have any concern about that proposal, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was just going to move to the prior testimonies of this witness. I was just referring to the statement and the attachments earlier, not to his prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. First we will receive in evidence the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Statement under 65 ter 02772, Your Honours, will be assigned P00851.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is there a list of these exhibits or are you going to move each one separately?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We would prefer to have the exhibits be part of the same exhibit numbers, so they've all been uploaded as one exhibit. If it will assist Your Honours, we can split them up and I can tender each one of them separately, but that was not our intention. They form one single exhibit presently in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Separate. It is more practical if it is separate, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Looking at the list on the screen of the court officer, there seem to be a large number. Is that something that can be dealt with administratively during our next break, Ms. Kravetz?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was just going to suggest that, Your Honour. I think that's the best way to proceed; it's a lengthy list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll do that. Already the first of those exhibits has been be exhibited in this trial. The remainder will be received, and the court officer, in liaison with you, will identify them and allocate numbers during the break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, did you previously testify before this Tribunal in the case of Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you had the chance before coming to court today to review the transcript of your testimony in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you also testify in the case of Milutinovic et al., in 2007, in March 2007?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And have you had the chance to review that transcript before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And sir, if you were asked today the same questions that you were asked in your prior testimony in the Milosevic case and Milutinovic case, would you provide the same answers today?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender both of these transcripts. The Milosevic transcript is 65 ter 02815, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That that will be assigned P00852, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Milutinovic transcript is 65 ter 05199, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now proceed to read the in-court summary for this witness. The witness is a retired Lieutenant-General in the Canadian Armed Forces. In November 1998 he was sent to Vienna to assist in the formation of the OSCE Verification Mission in Kosovo, KVM. He was later deployed to Kosovo and became the head of the KVM's regional centre in Prizren. The witness describes his staff with the KVM in Kosovo. The witness states that throughout KVM's time in Kosovo, Serb forces perpetrated frequent acts of intimidation, killings, as well as occasional shelling of villages with T-55 tanks, mortars, and Howitzers. He describes the coordination between MUP and VJ forces on the ground during joint operations. The witness met with several Serbian government officials during his time in Kosovo, and he describes these meetings. The witness also gives an account of the Racak incident of 15 January 1999. He describes his meetings with VJ and MUP officials in relation to this incident. The witness and other KVM personnel arrived in Racak after the incident took place, and he describes his observations in the village, including having seen bodies in the village. Once the NATO bombing campaign began, the witness became head of the KVM refugee task force in Albania. He coordinated with the Albanian government and various organisations in order to obtain the testimony of refugees coming into Albania. The witness describes the information obtained by his team during their interviews with the refugees. There were reports of systematic expulsions, mass killings, removal of ID cards, and widespread burning and plundering of Kosovo Albanian villages. That is the end of the in-court summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we have some minutes before the break, so I want to move to some aspects of your prior -- your statement and the attachments to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would ask with your leave that the usher provide a hard copy of the statement and the attachments, given that they are quite numerous, in order to ease reference of the witness. If that could be handed to the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, you stated earlier that during your time in Kosovo, you headed the KVM or the OSCE's regional office in Prizren. Just very briefly, could you explain what was the mandate of your office during the time you were there in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Basically, my mandate was within the boundaries of the regional centre which essentially followed along the boundaries of the -- of the southern region of the Prizren region of Kosovo, about one-fifth of the territory of Kosovo. The mandate was essentially to verify the accord between president Milosevic and Mr. Holbrooke that had been followed with a couple of subaccords with respect to the situation of the authority forces in Kosovo and the promotion of stability, if you wish, in the region. The idea was to ensure that there was a climate of normalcy as much as possible to enable a final political solution to be found to the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to a couple of subaccords to the main Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, and one of these is attached to your statement in the bundle you have before you is marked as MM1. And I would ask you to turn to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is, Your Honours, P836.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I would like to start with paragraph 1 of this agreement. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You've had the chance to recently review it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor please slow down and the witness as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we are reminded again to pause between question and answers. Since we are speaking the same language today, we need to stop before you answer the question. And I'll try to remember to do the same. Point 1 of this agreement, this understanding between KDOM and MUP or the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia, indicates that all check-points will be dismantled and that FRY authorities will establish 27 observation points and that one-third of these observation points will be manned initially. Could you explain to the Court your experience in implementing this first paragraph of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Essentially the mission, my portion of the mission tried to establish freedom of movement throughout our territory, throughout the area that we were covering. And to ensure that there were indeed no check-points. We frequently encountered them nevertheless, and at these check-points, of course, we tried to ensure the authorities were treating those that were being stopped with respect and with reasonable, if you wish, a reasonable approach. So this was -- this was an issue throughout my time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, with relation to the check-points that you said that you frequently encountered, who would usually be manning these check-points?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Usually the MUP police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the paragraph I referred to here in this agreement refers to observation points and one-third of these observation points being manned initially. Could you explain if you ever participated in any sort of verification with regard to that aspect, with respect to the observation points, the establishment of observation points?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Well, there's a fine line, I guess, between an observation point and a check-point. Presumably an observation point is where the observers or the people that are manning the observation point are strictly observing, whereas presumably those who are doing -- in a check-point, they would actually stop vehicles and personnel, and, you know, check -- do document checks and so on. So as I say, a fine line between that. We saw check-points frequently. Observation points, I guess, if you really think of a vehicle just being stopped with a couple police standing outside, that would count as an observation point where people would be observing what is going on. So that happened, I think, routinely. And my verifiers indeed verified that and saw it quite often. In terms of ensuring that there were exactly 27, and I, frankly, don't think we, certainly in our area, did not pay attention to that -- to the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And here it indicates that only one-third of these observation points were manned. How was that specific aspect verified?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It was not frankly. And this is one of the issues. Because the mission was -- took, you know, was only on the ground for a few months, we never had a chance to actually develop specific verification standards that could be given to our regional centre to -- and passed on to our personnel to ensure that they could go and check and make sure that, you know, the numbers that were specified were actually the numbers that were on the ground and so forth. So we never got to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Whenever you would observe or come across check-points or observation points, would this information be sent up to headquarters, the KVM headquarters in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it's the time for the break or I'm one minute ahead, but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On some views it could be called even three minutes, but I take the hint, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm looking -- I'm looking at my clock here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We take the hint, but we will resume at five minutes to 1.00. We must have a break now to enable tapes to be rewound, and we'll resume at five past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, we understand the group of exhibits is taking a little longer to resolve than expected. We will continue leaving it to be resolved once we adjourn for today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just on that point, Your Honour, I had indicated when I was tendered the statement that there were three attachments that I did not seek to tender. I understand from Your Honours' instructions that those three attachments will not be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood that you were accepting Mr. Djurdjic's suggestion that all the be exhibits should be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have to double-check. I believe that those were not used in the Milutinovic case, but I will have to double-check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Check that, if they were used in the Milutinovic case, they should be received. That's where we are at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence agrees with any decision about exhibits if they have been used before, our proposal stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're in a very cooperative mood, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, before we -- at the break, we were discussing attachment 1 to your statement, which is the agreement between KDOM and the Serbian MUP, also known as the Byrnes-Djordjevic agreement. Before we turn back to that, I just wanted to clarify and answer you gave earlier when I was asking you about the mandate of your office. You said that you understood the mandate to be the verification of the implementation of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement and subsequent accords. How did you understand you were to carry out this mandate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: We carried that out through patrolling. Patrolling widely throughout the region. By ensuring that we had good contact and regular contact with all the authorities and all the parties in the area, the local people as well. We ensured that we created a climate of trust and of normalcy, as I said before. And we ensured the protection of human rights by, you know, being there when there were incidents going on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. If we could now turn back to the document you have there before you, and if we could focus now on number 2 of that document, which refers to incidents of increased tension: "The police will have the right upon not to find KDOM/OSCE to perform patrol duties and armour vehicles with machine-guns et cetera. An [indiscernible] which will be used exclusively in self-defence with restraint?" Could you tell us, based on your experience on the ground, how this point of the agreement was implemented, if it was at all? And I'm specifically interested in the notification aspect of this clause of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: This -- an aspect I would say that the -- in terms of notification, seldom were we notified when there would be patrols in armoured vehicles outside of the normal zones. There were some patrols that we were used to doing that we knew that the MUP would be doing, and there was no problem. That went on regularly. And some of those were in armoured vehicles. But if there was a -- it they were patrolling areas that they wanted to do without -- in areas that were not their regular one, I guess, we seldom were notified of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned earlier that part of your duties included contact with authorities and all parties. Now, with respect to this specific issue of notification, was this a matter you raised with MUP authorities when you -- when it wasn't complied with?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Whenever there were issues of -- of -- issues with the authorities, we definitely raised them. I can't remember any specific -- any specific issues or points that were raised from that point of view after ten years, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Now, if we could look at paragraph 3 of this agreement, it speaks about police withdrawal of its stationary forces, and there are a series of localities which are listed there. When you arrived to Kosovo, were you provided with any sort of base-line of the numbers of police forces that were to be on -- or were authorised to be on the ground in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were you able to verify whether this aspects of the agreement was complied with, the withdrawal of police from the stationary forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Again this is an aspect that we did not get to appoint where we would receive the standards and the base-line, if you wish, of forces that were meant to be in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So are you saying that you were not able to verify whether there had been a compliance with paragraph 3 of this agreement because you were not provided with the information by the MUP, would that be an understanding of the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct. So because of that we went from the understanding that the forces that were there on the ground, we wanted to ensure that there was no reinforcement while we were deployed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My apologies again for that. I know we are going a bit fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were you able then to ensure whether there were any reinforcements of MUP units on ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: We -- we continued patrolling. We ensured that we had good contact with the authorities. And, of course, we were also in contact with the locals who would tell us if they saw an increased presence in particular areas to enable us to follow through. So through this programme of patrolling, this programme of contact with the authorities and with the locals, we had a pretty good sense of whether major forces were actually -- would actually have come into the province.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you are talking about major forces coming into the province, are you speaking about regular MUP units, or other types of police units?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would say all types of units, regular and perhaps special.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you frequently observe special types of police units on the ground when you were conducting your verifications?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: On a few occasions we did report some special units, and we noticed that they were special units because they were usually dressed in different types of dress, different types of uniforms, than the regular MUP units which were in dark blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And when you were -- on the occasions that you observed these units, was there anything -- anything else different about them other than their uniform from their regular police units that you had the opportunity to see?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would say that the -- their behaviour was reportedly at times more arrogant and in fact they -- usually these special units would be quite scary for the locals. The local people were usually quite afraid of them thinking that perhaps they were members of special units that were brought in for special duties. So just by their behaviour and by the fact that they would be in a particular area that had the -- often the impact of -- or the effect of scaring the locals or worrying the locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And on the occasions that you were able to come across these special units, would you -- would they be carrying any sort of task that would be different from regular police units that you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I can think of one of the Rogovo incident, for example, where they were usually in -- when I saw them they were, of course, looking at the postmortem and what had happened in the area. I don't know exactly what involvement they had during the actual incident, but certainly when I came upon the scene, they were -- they were around, and they were looking after, you know, the aftermath of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you a question - now that we are speaking about MUP units - a question about your statement. And this is at paragraph 18, on page 6 of the statement in the English; and I believe it's page 5 on the B/C/S. You refer to VJ and MUP, and you say there were frequent intimidations, killings, and occasional shelling of villages by T-55 tanks, mortars, and Howitzers and by the VJ. And then you say MUPs were the front-runners in any action and the VJ appeared to have colluded or provided heavy fire support on several occasions. Can you explain how it is that you came to that conclusion that MUP were the front-runners in any action and VJ seemed to be providing heavy fire support?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. In both the instances where I personally witnessed the events and those that were reported to me by my verifiers, which I take as being true reporting and accurate factual reporting, it seemed to us or the tendency was for us to see an increased presence of MUP which would deploy out of their -- out of their barracks and be on the scene. And then usually the VJ would stand a little further out and seemed to provide - and again this is a sense of an assessment of the manner in which operations would be conducted - the VJ would seem to provide a kind of perimeter to the activity. So this is what I mean about the -- about the precursors. The MUP were usually the front-runners, they would arrive on the scene. And then eventually the VJ would deploy in kind of a perimeter position. This is, in fact, the assessment that I made with respect to the Racak incident specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We will move to the Racak incident in a minute. Before getting to that, just to clarify the answer, you said that you saw an increased presence of MUP which would deploy out of their barracks and be on the scene. Were these occasions when you saw increased presence of MUP out of barracks, were these sort of deployments authorised or as you understood pursuant to the agreements, the agreement we just saw and the other agreements that were signed and gave you a mandate for verification?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, they were not. Though, I must add that they were often provoked into these -- into these deployments. Specifically, for example, in an incident near the small town of Randubrava, which is near Prizren, which happened fairly close to the end of my time in Kosovo, there was an incident of some firing and entire company of MUP actually deployed to -- to look after -- to react to the activity; and after some discussion and some negotiations, they returned to their barracks. But this is kind of the -- very often they were provoked into doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in situations like this based on the terms we saw of the agreement we were just looking at, and moving specifically to paragraph 2, would this be an instance where the requirement would be provide prior notification to you before carrying out such type of deployment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would say this would be an instance where they should provide advanced notice. Although, I will again couch that by saying that there are times when, if provoked, it would be understandable; and since my verifiers were on the ground and often I was as well, that it would be understandable that the deployment would happen and that we would make contact on the ground with the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this provocation in paragraph 18, again, this is the same paragraph I was reading from earlier, you say: "Generally when provoked or perceived to be provoked, the reaction of the VJ and the MUP was disproportionate to the provocation or alleged attack by the KLA." Can you explain what you mean by that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say in this case, this was a regular reaction by the authority forces. That sometimes a fairly minor incident, although it's difficult to say what's a major incident and what's a minor incident, but let's just say that the usual reaction from the VJ and the MUP was usually quite disproportionate, that is, much stronger than the provocation or attack by the other side. That seemed to be the typical reaction there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you give us an example of what you mean when you say it was disproportionate or much stronger?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Certainly. Coming back to the Randubrava incident, the incident was in the small, small town. There seemed to be a couple or three -- some fighters that were taking actually pot-shots, and that -- and from that small incident, an entire company of MUP was deployed on the ground in armoured vehicles. So an entire company of course is about 100, 120 personnel. So that's an example of the type of reaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And do you recall the date of this incident that you are referring to, just approximately when it happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I think it was towards the end of February. I believe it was towards the end of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That would be --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: 1999. It might even have been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask to you look at the screen and wait for the cursor to stop before starting your answer, so that we cannot overlap between question and answer. So I was just asking you about the date of the incident.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would say that it was probably towards the end of February 1999 or it may even have been in March of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you talk about entire company of MUP deployed to the ground, are you speak being regular police officers or these special units that you were describing earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: These would have been regular police units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned -- referred to the Racak incident; and I know it's also discussed in your statement in previous testimony. I have a couple of questions just to clarify some aspects of your written evidence on this incident. In paragraph 34 of your statement, you say that when the incident -- Racak incident took place, you were in Pec/Peja and that you returned later that afternoon after receiving reports from your personnel. Do you recall what exactly you were told had happened in Racak and when it was, I mean, which date you are referring to specifically?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th of January, 1999, we had been at a meeting of the entire KVM in terms of a meeting of the operational commanders and so on, and so all the representatives of the different regional centres were meeting in Pec/Peja and we were, you know, discussing issues and coordinating work. During that -- during the day on the 15th, we received reports that there was a -- an action going on in the area of Racak. At this point, Racak was outside of my Regional Centre 1. It was in Regional Centre 5's area. And Regional Centre 5 had no commander at the time. They had -- they had a deputy commander, but the commander had not been deployed yet into the regional centre. So at this point, General Drewienkiewicz, General DZ, asked me if I would be able to actually deploy to Regional Centre 5's area - and, of course, the deputy commander was with me in Pec/Peja, so he was aware of this - and to see if I could take a couple of my patrols from my area and deploy there to Racak, which is what I did at the end of the day on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, just going back a little bit, you say that during the day of the 15th, you received report that there was an action going on. From whom did you receive these reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: From the verifiers of Regional Centre 5, from those that were on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So were there verifiers actually at Racak at the time when this action was happening?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did they tell you was going on in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: They were reporting that there was a -- there was some firing going on. That there was -- there seemed to be an attack going on in the village. Now, I don't remember exactly what the tenure of their comments was, but that there was an action going on in the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find the passage that you discussed right now with the witness about RC 5 verifiers in Racak. If I could just get a reference, the number of the paragraph, because I don't see anything like that in paragraph 34.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That was additional information that the witness provided, and I was asking for him to elaborate on what was in paragraph 34 of the statement and this is additional information that the witness just provided. Paragraph 34 is on page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's in elaboration of paragraph 34, Mr. Djurdjic. Additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But in that case, I believe it would be in keeping with the rules for direct examination of a live witness, and I don't believe such leading questions are appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Take notice, please, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. I was just asking him to elaborate on what was in the statement. That's all. And I don't believe I put a leading question, but I do take Your Honours's guidance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are grateful. Just carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that you went to Racak that day. What, if anything, were you able to observe in the village when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I arrived in the dusk, dusk was falling at this point and so I decided to go directly to -- to the hospital to see -- to meet there with the folks that were on the ground from Regional Centre 5. And indeed we -- they had begun to -- they had begun to -- to bring out some of the casualties. Some of the local people who had been shot and hurt. So that was the -- that's what I observed that night in -- on the night of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were the observers who were on the ground from Regional Centre 5 able to provide you any additional information to what they had seen happening at Racak that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was indeed the time when I was told about the action going on in the city of Racak, that some of my -- some of these personnel from Regional Centre 5 had been on the hills and had seen tanks firing into -- into the town, that had seen personnel or MUP personnel going into -- into the city, into the town. But that's the point at which I was told exactly what had happened. I was told what had happened generally, I mean, in the city of Racak, in the town of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say that your -- the personnel, KVM personnel was from Regional Centre 5 had been up on the hills and was able to observe this. Had they been -- did you receive any reports of whether there had been any outgoing fire from Racak to this tank position that you said was firing into the village?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, actually and this is one thing that we couldn't really understand. By our understanding, Racak had not been a stronghold of the KLA. This seemed to be to us something that was very, you know, very unprovoked; and so we could not understand why there had been such a huge presence and a huge action in Racak, why this had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you refer to having arrived to the village and seeing casualties brought out. Do you recall approximately how many victims you saw, and if you can say anything about the victims, the age, whether female or male?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I believe at one point in my statement I do give some details of the -- of the casualties; but I do remember, myself, being in the hospital and seeing a woman and a young girl that were brought in exactly at the time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you later return to Racak at any point in the following days?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. After giving direction to my verifiers and to those of Regional Centre 5 to maintain a presence, as much as possible overnight, I returned to my headquarters and came back in the morning. My verifiers came onto the ground at 7.00, and then I arrived about 9.00 into the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who accompanied you on that second occasion when you visited the village?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I was accompanied as usually but my driver and actually by a young lady who was my Serbian interpreter because I had intended also to go visit the brigade commander from the brigade responsible for that area to find out what happened, to liaise with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, what were you able to observe when you arrived at 9.00 a.m. in the village on 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: When I arrived, I went into the village and was able to observe a couple of bodies before, you know, I wanted to actually go and see a few bodies on my own, and then to get a sense of what was going on in the village. Of course, I also spoke to my verifiers and then made my way in towards the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to meet with the brigade commander that day, the brigade commander in charge of that area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I was not. When I arrived at the meeting, I was greeted by the liaison officer from the brigade, and I had a discussion with him and he told me, and I think this is in the statement, about the fact that his brigade commander was not available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the minutes of this meeting are an attachment to your statement. This is attachment 8, and I would ask you to please turn to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is in e-court page 83 of the English, and page 99 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you on that page?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the notes of this meeting indicate that a Lieutenant-Colonel Pera Petrovic was present. Is this the person that you were referring to as being the liaison officer of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this meeting that you had at the brigade headquarters with Colonel Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The aim of the meeting was to find out why this activity, this incident had taken place, why vehicles, tanks, and so on had been firing into what we thought was a completely empty village, a village of civilians. And this seemed to me to be a disregard for the agreement, keeping the troops in barracks and also keeping the situation normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the minutes record you saying, and this is at the top next to "M," which I understand stands for your name --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- record you saying: "Your tanks, heavy artillery, mortars, and AV moved out of barracks one week ago in complete violation of the agreement and are still out and VJ will not cooperate with KVM." Are these tanks and heavy artillery mortars that you are referring to equipment that had been deployed to the area of Racak one week before? Or where exactly had this deployment been made in violation of the agreement, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Now, this, you have to bear in mind that this brigade and this area was outside of my regional centre, so these statements came as a result of my discussions with Gil Gilbertson who is the deputy head of the Regional Centre 5. They had their observers -- their verifiers had observed these deployments outside of the barracks by the VJ and MUP. So in this case, I'm sorry, by the VJ. And so this is -- this is what I'm referring to. I had received that information from Mr. Gilbertson who was with me at this meeting. I do recall, though, that there was one particular area where there was a deployment of -- seemed to be a deployment of artillery pieces near the road near Racak that had been contested by the KVM and, I believe, protested by Regional Centre 5. This is before Racak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And this deployment of artillery pieces near Racak, this was not an authorised deployment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: From my understanding, no, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was the VJ -- did the VJ have any artillery positions in the Stimlje area that were authorised pursuant to the agreements, if you recall? I know this was not your specific area of responsibility, but based on what you know from that area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. Now, if we go down a bit further in these notes, we have Colonel Petrovic indicating that "Stimlje was done by the MUP with PRAHA AVs and one tank don't know how they were dealing with it." Based on what you were able to observe of how the MUP operated, did they usually have any tanks at their disposal when they carried out action?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, as I said earlier, it seemed to us that they regularly enlisted the support of tanks. Now, we knew pretty well that the MUP had no tanks within their inventory, so we certainly thought that the tanks were provided by the VJ. But it seemed routine to us throughout my time there that the VJ and MUP would work in coordination. I believe, as I said in one of my statements, my assessment is that they each had their chain of command, direct chain of command to each other, parallel chain of command, I should say, the MUP and the VJ; but they definitely coordinated regularly during actions. And, of course, as a military man, this is just a regular and routine procedure that you would never have two forces, friendly forces, which are working on the same side operating in the same zone without ensuring that you have good coordination to make sure that there are no engagement of friendly forces, any friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you had told us earlier that your observers had seen tank firing into the village. When you went there on the 15th or on the 16th, did you see any evidence that a tank had been deployed in the area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: There is one incident, of course, that I've spoken about on a couple of occasions, and that is in my statement, where one of the verifiers specifically had told me that he stood beside a tank that had been firing into a house, that had been occupied by civilians, and when that tank actually stopped firing, that they went into the house and helped the people to come out. And I subsequently, on the 16th, went to that hill where the tank had been reported and saw tank tracks on that hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the minutes here record you asking "who coordinated tank fire on civilian houses where no persons were firing back." Is this the same incident that you are just speaking about that your observers were able to see happening?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you raised with Colonel Petrovic at this meeting that this had been an unauthorized move from barracks and the notes have an exclamation point and the answer that is recorded here from Colonel Petrovic is "we are authorised for the staffs, my commander will see you in the evening." What did you understand based from this meeting had been the VJ involvement in this action?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I certainly thought that in his view, in Petrovic's view, the movement out of barracks and the firing and so on had been from what he thought were normal tasks. I also understood that at this point that I would have a chance to meet the commander on the Sunday evening, and I don't know exactly what day of the week this was, but. So he certainly, I think, felt that this was a -- that this was an authorised and normal activity, where we felt that it was not. That it was unauthorized.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we turn the page, we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is page 84 in e-court of the English, and page 100 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The third line from the top, if you could just explain what is written there. It starts with "If provoked with SA..."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. This -- the point I was trying to make here that proportional force should be used in any reaction to an incident, i.e., if you are provoked with small arms, then you would use small arms. SA was my note writer's abbreviation for small arms. Trying to make the fact that artillery use in this case was disproportionate use of force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You refer to, you say like Racak and Petrovo. Do you recall exactly had happened at Petrovo, you have been explaining what occurred in Racak but.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I don't, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. I understand that that same day you also met with representatives from the local MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the notes of these -- this meeting is -- are also attached and they are attachment 13, that's MM13. There are three copies of the notes of this meeting attached to your statement. I understand that the operative one is the last one which is the signed version; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct. What usually happened is my notetaker would draft the notes and send them in to me, and usually with one draft I was able to correct some of the issues and give it back to him and I would sign them. In this case, I guess it means it took two drafts before I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that this meeting took place again on the 16th of January, and it was held at the MUP headquarters in Urosevac. And in attendance are Colonel Janicevic, chief of the secretariat, MUP. Would this be the Secretariat of Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we also see that Mr. Gilbertson and an interpreter were present at this meeting. And what was the aim of this meeting with Colonel Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The aim there was exactly the same one as with the VJ. It was to find out exactly what had happened and what had provoked and what had made them undertake this action in Racak. To find out who, in fact, was in charge of the operation and who had, you know, the cooperation between the MUP and the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the minutes record Mr. Janicevic saying that - and this is towards the middle bottom part of the page - started action at 0330, ended at 1530. And later, Mr. Gilbertson asked who ordered this to happen, and there are a series of answers which are marked as evasive answer here in the minutes. Based on your discussions with Colonel Janicevic at the meetings, what impressions did you form as to who had ordered this action to take place at Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: My sense was that he was trying to be quite evasive in terms of who exactly was in charge. We asked him on several occasions. We were trying to establish exactly who was the person in charge. And you know, we wanted, as much as possible, to know what the facts were. But my sense certainly was that he was -- he was the one in charge of these policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we turn the page this is page 104 in the English in e-court, and page 117 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Gilbertson is asking him how many police officers were involved, and Mr. Janicevic says 100 men. Later towards the bottom of the notes here you say you were in charge of 100 policemen, and he responds, If it is your concern, yes. And Mr. Gilbertson asked, he says, We just left the VJ, that put all the blame on you, were they with you or not? And he responds, We were not with the VJ. Was that your understanding of how the action had happened? That Mr. Janicevic, was -- I mean, was your understanding consistent with what Mr. Janicevic was saying that the MUP was involved in this action without any participation from the region?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I certainly thought that Mr. Janicevic was quite an erudite gentleman and able to, I think, answer questions in a rather kind of roundabout way. And certainly that's the reason why I wanted to ask him if indeed he was in charge of the 100 hundred policemen and I think we wore him down to finally tell us yes. But in terms of the VJ, I think I could have taken his answer at the time and you know, to the best of my recollection that his answer could have been, you know, we were not with the VJ when we did the assault, this does not mean perhaps that he would have had the VJ in support of his -- of the action. So you, you know, I mean, to me it left some, you know, some room for interpretation here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say it left some room for interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, that perhaps the VJ were involved, but if they were my assessment was that the VJ would have been in the perimeter position around the -- around the -- the town of Racak, this would not necessarily mean that the VJ would be in the town with the MUP, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And was what Mr. Janicevic told you at this meeting consistent with what your KVM observers had seen on the ground happen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, it was not. As I mentioned and as I assessed, I believe that the VJ was indeed involved both from the point of view of support from the perimeter and firing into the city, into the town, and you know, in those deployments such as that artillery position. So they were indeed involved in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's the end of the session. I have more questions for you, General, but we will have to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, General, because the courtroom is used by another Chamber now. We must adjourn for the day and resume at 9.00 in the morning. And will hope to have satisfactory progress tomorrow, even final, even.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We adjourn until --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on that note, I would like to point out that the witness has indicated that he needs to leave by Friday morning, so I will make my best to make progress tomorrow, but I also wanted to let Your Honours know that we do need to complete this witness by early Friday morning at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to greet you upon adjournment. That's why I stood up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very gracious of you, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will be watching your time in the morning very closely, Ms. Kravetz, because Mr. Djurdjic must have time to cross-examine the general. So time will be given close attention. The court officer will be giving exhibit numbers to all the exhibits that were tendered earlier, including the ones you initially did not seek to tender but which we understand are all being admitted by consent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, we resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
